title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Manchester Airports Group refuses a ransom after data on 8.7 million customers is stolen — flight operations untouched
items.content_text: Manchester Airports Group, which runs Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands, confirmed on 27 August that attackers accessed data belonging to roughly 8.7 million customers over the weekend of 22–23 August. MAG says it detected the intrusion on 25 August, that a ransom was demanded and refused, and that no payment card details were taken. Crucially, the group states flight operations, passenger safety and aviation security were unaffected. The stolen records come from car park, lounge, Fast Track and airport Wi-Fi systems — commercial platforms sitting well away from the airfield. That separation is the story: it is what kept the Collins Aerospace outage of September 2025 from repeating here, and it is exactly the boundary most airport groups have never formally tested.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Manchester Airports Group statement carried by BBC News, Cybernews and Security Magazine; passenger counts and data categories as stated by MAG
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusion dated to 22–23 Aug 2026; detected 25 Aug 2026; publicly disclosed 27 Aug 2026

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored platforms that scanned critical infrastructure and relayed attacks through hijacked devices
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan handled reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, including NASA, and the described activity runs back to at least 2018. For airports and airlines the relay layer is the transferable lesson: a terminal building is dense with small, internet-connected, unowned devices, and source addresses in your logs never proved anything.
tags: Incident — Law-enforcement seizure of state-sponsored attack infrastructure

items.title: Ransomware took out door access, elevators and HVAC monitoring at a major hospital — read it as a terminal-building scenario
items.content_text: Health Sciences Centre in Winnipeg, Manitoba’s largest hospital, reported a ransomware incident on 10 August that disabled facility management systems including central HVAC monitoring, elevators, door access and ID card operations. Staff moved to local monitoring and manual workarounds; clinical services continued and no patient impact was indicated. The ransomware group, initial access route and whether data was taken have not been confirmed. Airport operators should read this as the closest available analogue to their own environment. Access control, elevators, HVAC and the systems behind them are not back-office IT — in a terminal they gate passenger flow, secure airside boundaries and keep equipment rooms within temperature limits.
tags: Incident — Ransomware reaching building management OT

items.title: Clop names more than 40 PTC Windchill victims, with aerospace among the confirmed sectors
items.content_text: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations as victims of a campaign against internet-facing PTC Windchill product lifecycle management deployments, with aerospace, manufacturing and industrial suppliers among the confirmed names. Windchill holds design files, bills of material, supplier documentation and change history. For airlines and MRO organisations the exposure is largely indirect but specific: component and airframe suppliers keep configuration, service bulletin and modification records in systems of this kind, and a leak reveals not only design detail but which operators fly which configuration. Ask suppliers what they hold on you rather than waiting to see it published.
tags: Incident — PLM supply-chain campaign naming aerospace victims

items.title: Treasury sanctions an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
items.content_text: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels, with a related State Department reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. Aviation is not named. What makes it relevant is that the tradecraft described — harvesting credentials, exploiting vendor footholds, collecting network documentation — transfers directly, and airports and airlines carry an unusually large population of third parties with standing access.
tags: Incident — Nation-state targeting of US critical infrastructure

items.title: An AI model re-targeted a working PLC exploit onto a second controller in hours — and destroyed one
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For airport and airline ground systems the point is variant coverage. Baggage handling, jet bridges, fuelling, de-icing and airfield lighting are typically controlled by close relatives of the same controller families, and “that advisory named a different model” has been quietly carrying a lot of deferred risk.
tags: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques, and it landed the same day Manchester Airports Group disclosed its breach — a coincidence of timing, not a link. Aviation is not called out, but the exposure the NCSC describes is the airport’s: a campus estate of controllers bought as part of a building fit-out, supported remotely by an OEM, and rarely re-surveyed. Baggage handling drives, jet bridge controllers, de-icing and fuelling telemetry, airfield lighting cabinets, stand equipment, BMS and access control all sit in that category, and the instruction not to assume they are unreachable from the internet without verifying it is the whole point of the alert.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
items.content_text: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Airports recognise this immediately: common-use passenger processing, baggage systems, building management and corporate IT frequently share one Active Directory, monitoring is often contracted out, and the facility side of the estate is regularly excluded from whatever detection exists.

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers on exposed networks
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to turn a well-documented open-source S7 library into custom tooling that queries internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic resembling legitimate monitoring. The agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning. Aviation is not a named sector, but SIMATIC controllers are common in airport facility systems: baggage handling, jet bridges, de-icing and fuel farms, airfield lighting auxiliaries and central plant. The change worth absorbing is that protocol knowledge no longer limits who can interrogate a controller, so obscurity is a weaker control than it was.

items.title: 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter, and none of them needed the control system touched
items.content_text: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up roughly 12 percent on the first, and made the point that attackers do not need control-system access to disrupt operations. Aviation has demonstrated the same principle repeatedly: check-in, boarding and baggage disruption at major European hubs came from a shared passenger-processing platform, not from anything airside. The systems that stop an airport are the common-use platforms, resource management, baggage reconciliation and crew scheduling, and those rarely get the segmentation and restoration testing applied to safety-critical equipment.

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
items.content_text: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is an aviation product, and after the MAG breach and the Collins Aerospace outage of last September that is the recurring lesson: aviation disruption arrives through the ordinary IT layer. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the baggage-handling control server, BMS front end, CCTV recorder, flight information display controller and OT network sensor in most terminals are Linux underneath — typically vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s schedule. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory, relevant wherever firmware or software for terminal or ground equipment is staged. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; instances still exposed usually belong to nobody.
tags: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue

items.title: A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
items.content_text: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. At an airport the exposure sits under the airport operational database and the reporting tier around it — baggage handling event and tracking data, gate and stand allocation, access-control and CCTV management servers, building management historians, and the fuelling and de-icing records that facilities teams keep. On the airline and MRO side it is the maintenance and parts systems. These are commonly SQL Server instances installed by a systems integrator and never revisited. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, historian and MES databases

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. Airports and airlines run NetScaler heavily because so many users are third parties — handlers, contractors, MRO providers and airline staff needing access to airport systems.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access

items.title: Two unauthenticated flaws in Veeam ONE 13 — the monitoring layer that watches the backups you would restore from
items.content_text: Veeam disclosed vulnerabilities in Veeam ONE 13 in knowledge-base articles published on 25 August. CVE-2026-64633 is rated CVSS v4.0 10.0 and allows remote, unauthenticated code execution on the Veeam ONE agent host; CVE-2026-65641 is rated 9.3 and lets a remote unauthenticated attacker coerce SMB authentication out of the Veeam ONE service account, which is the first step in relaying that account somewhere more useful. Veeam ONE 13.x is affected and the 12.x line is not. At an airport Veeam ONE is frequently the console watching backups of the facility and operations servers — access control, video management, BMS and the baggage handling controllers’ configuration — which is precisely the recovery capability that mattered in the hospital ransomware case on this page, where door access, elevators and HVAC monitoring all went down together. There is no report of exploitation yet, but backup and monitoring servers are a standing target precisely because compromising them removes the recovery option before the ransomware runs.
tags: Advisory — Backup and monitoring infrastructure, unauthenticated

items.title: A Git server exploit in KEV — and it is often where facility system configuration lives
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, the flaw lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July, so exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea appears in airport engineering and systems groups because it is straightforward to stand up for baggage system configuration, lighting and BMS programs, integration scripts and display templates. A modest contractor account then becomes code execution on the machine holding operational configuration. Federal remediation was due 28 August.

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: critical code execution in Siveillance VMS, maximum severity in IoT2050
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in its August set alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact, with CISA issuing companion ICS advisories the same week. Two matter most in a terminal environment. A maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced allows unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges. A critical code execution issue was also fixed in Siveillance video management servers — and airport CCTV is not a nice-to-have: it is evidence, it is part of the security programme, and its servers usually sit on the same network as access control.
tags: Advisory — August ICS Patch Tuesday, Siemens estate

items.title: A hard-coded key in Johnson Controls Airwall — the product many sites use to protect everything else
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-03 republishes a Johnson Controls advisory covering a hard-coded cryptographic key in Airwall, alongside an arbitrary file read issue. Airwall is a micro-segmentation and secure-remote-access product deployed precisely to isolate building systems and broker vendor access, and Johnson Controls products are widespread across airport facilities. A weakness in a compensating control deserves more attention than the same weakness elsewhere, because the design assumes this device holds. Where Airwall separates corporate IT from terminal building systems or brokers contractor access to them, this is not a routine patch.
tags: Advisory — Hard-coded key in a segmentation product

items.title: No login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-06 covers the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, whose web management interface does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative functionality. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read configuration, change settings, hijack sessions or disrupt operation. CISA notes the vendor acknowledged the reports, said a patch was in development, then stopped responding. Inexpensive serial converters like this are scattered through airport estates, sitting behind older fuel meters, de-icing rigs, weather and lighting equipment, gate systems and standby generators — installed because something legacy needed a network drop, and rarely recorded afterwards.
tags: Advisory — Serial-to-Ethernet gateway, no vendor patch

items.title: Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
items.content_text: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage.
tags: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force

_otthreatfeed.category: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; not yet in force — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA publishes internet exposure reduction guidance — and the target list for this sector is terminal building-management and baggage-handling controllers, airfield lighting and de-icing telemetry, jet-bridge and fuelling systems, and OEM support links into all of them
items.content_text: CISA released guidance on 26 August directing organisations to identify which of their systems are reachable from the internet, remove remote access that is not required, and harden whatever must stay externally accessible. It is deliberately unglamorous: an inventory step, a removal step and a hardening step, published in the same week the UK NCSC warned that internet-exposed OT and edge devices are being targeted with real-world disruption already caused. Airport facility OT is a patchwork of vendor-maintained subsystems, each with its own support arrangement, sitting on a network that grew by accretion around a passenger-facing IT estate. Exposure in this sector usually turns up in the systems nobody lists as OT. The guidance carries no deadline and applies to no one by force, which is precisely why it tends to be filed rather than executed.
tags: Guidance — Internet exposure reduction for IT, OT and ICS

items.title: From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware, with fuller reporting to follow. Airports and airlines are mainly buyers here rather than obligated manufacturers, and that is the useful angle: the suppliers of baggage systems, common-use platforms, jet bridges, lighting controls and building management equipment sold into Europe acquire a defined notification duty that can be written into support contracts.
tags: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation

_otthreatfeed.category: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation

items.title: The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys
items.content_text: ISASecure announced a partnership with the National Security Agency to develop a High Criticality Component Security Assurance certification scheme, derived from its Component Security Assurance programme and grounded in ISA/IEC 62443-4-2. Once accepted, the NSA intends to use it when adding OT components to the National Security Systems product compliant list. Airports are not the target market, but the mechanism matters: a large buyer making certification a purchase condition changes what vendors build, and that language migrates into other specifications. For an authority writing a baggage system, lighting control or BMS tender, it is a citable standard rather than an invented requirement.

_otthreatfeed.category: Policy — Procurement-driven security certification

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026
